evals.prompt: Write the business case for replacing our homegrown support ticket router at Northwind. Today 40 agents each spend about 20 minutes a day manually re-routing misassigned tickets (from a two-week time study). Loaded agent cost is $45/hour. Options on the table: build a ML router (estimate 3 engineers for 2 quarters), buy a vendor tool (Vendor X quoted $60k/year, year-two price unknown), or keep things as they are. The same 3 engineers would otherwise ship the self-serve billing portal. The VP of Support decides by November 15.
assertions: The first lines state the ask — option, cost, benefit range, and the November 15 deadline — in under 40 words
Option 0 (do nothing) is present and costed using the user's 40 agents x 20 min/day x $45/hour figures
Every benefit is a re-runnable calculation with formula, sourced inputs, and a confidence tag (high/medium/low)
Outputs such as ROI and payback are ranges with a stated lean, not single-point figures like '327% ROI'
Each option shows build, run, and opportunity cost, with the displaced work named as the self-serve billing portal
The vendor's unknown year-two price is called out as an unknown or flagged assumption, not filled with an invented number
Names the flip-assumption that would reverse the recommendation, with a de-risking step if its confidence is low
Recommends exactly one option and states the runner-up's strongest argument fairly

evals.prompt: The board of our food bank network needs to decide whether to get a refrigerated van. Everything I have is in hollin_vale_inputs.md. Write the business case for the November 20 board meeting. Keep it to what fits on two printed pages — the board reads it on paper.
assertions: Uses the warehouse log's total (about 10.4 tonnes a year) for spoilage, or explicitly reconciles it against the chair's 18-tonne figure, rather than silently using 18 tonnes
Catches that the lease quote's annual figure is wrong: $1,850 x 12 is $22,200, not $19,200

Recognises that the grant can fund only the van purchase, so the lease and all running costs (including the paid driver) must come from the $20,000-a-year operating headroom, and notes that even the buy option's recurring costs (about $33,500 a year) exceed that headroom
Treats keeping the volunteer drivers as a real option to compare against, and accounts for 3 of the 11 regular drivers leaving by spring
Does not present a number of extra families fed as a sourced fact; any conversion from produce to families is flagged as an assumption not in the input, or the gap is named
Does not invent costs, funding sources, or figures not in the input file without labelling them as assumptions
Fits roughly two printed pages (about 1,000 words or less) and makes a clear recommendation the board can vote on

evals.prompt: my dental practice is thinking about getting one of those 3D intraoral scanners for crowns instead of goopy impressions, its like $30k?? my partner thinks its a waste of money. we do maybe 8 crowns a month. can you give me a few bullets on whether its worth it, dont need an essay
assertions: Gives a usable answer on whether the scanner is worth it instead of only asking questions back
Stays to a few bullets — no more than about 10 bullets or 250 words
Compares buying against keeping traditional impressions, not just the scanner's benefits in isolation
Any figures the user did not give (lab fees, chair time saved, impression material costs, financing) are labelled as estimates or assumptions, not stated as facts
Names what the answer most depends on (for example, savings per crown or crown volume) so the owner knows what to check before deciding
Written in plain language for a dentist, without unexplained finance jargon such as NPV or IRR
